title: Hazel and the Inventory
premise: After her mother's funeral, Juniper Delacroix drifts through the estate like a tenant, cataloging objects she cannot bring herself to name. When the childhood house on Hazel Street goes up for auction, Juniper discovers her mother had been quietly paying off a debt owed to the family who once sheltered them — and that the auction will erase the last place where the truth of their estrangement lives. Returning to the house before the sale, Juniper finds Hazel Okafor, the childhood friend her mother never spoke of again, still living next door with her own grievances. Together they excavate the silence: a fire, a betrayal, a sacrifice made in secret. In the end, Juniper lets the house go to auction but claims what no ledger can hold — Hazel's forgiveness, and a found family built on told truths rather than inherited ones.
about_author: Silas Fairweather is the pen name of a former probate clerk who spent eleven years cataloging other people's unfinished lives before turning to fiction. They write about inheritance, silence, and the small justices families arrange for themselves when the law looks away.

chapters.title: The Tenant
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Three weeks after the funeral, Juniper inventories their mother's apartment room by room, unable to decide what to keep or discard. The emotional beat is numb displacement — grief experienced as paperwork.

chapters.title: A Letter Addressed to No One
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Among the papers, Juniper finds bank statements showing monthly payments to an unknown recipient for nineteen years, stopping only at the mother's death. The beat is the first crack of mystery: the mother they mourned was someone else entirely.

chapters.title: Hazel Street, Lot 14
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. An auction notice arrives: the childhood house is being sold to settle the mother's 'outstanding obligations.' Juniper drives out and sees the house for the first time in two decades. The beat is dread mixed with involuntary homesickness.

chapters.title: The Woman Next Door
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. On the porch of the neighboring house sits Hazel Okafor, older, wary, unmistakable. She recognizes Juniper instantly; Juniper barely remembers her. The beat is the vertigo of being remembered more than you remember.

chapters.title: What the Fire Took
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel recalls the night of the fire twenty-two years ago — the Okafor garage burned, her father's workshop destroyed, and Juniper's mother appearing at dawn with money and a warning never to speak of it. The beat is smoldering resentment finally given air.

chapters.title: Inventory of Small Mercies
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Back in the apartment, Juniper re-reads the inventory differently, matching each object to fragments of memory from Hazel Street. The beat is the slow horror of realizing the mother's whole life was organized around one concealed event.

chapters.title: The Auctioneer's Terms
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper meets the auctioneer, Ms. Voss, who reveals the sale was initiated by a creditor — someone has been pressing the estate since the funeral. The beat is paranoia: the silence had a witness all along.

chapters.title: Nineteen Years of Tuesdays
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel shows Juniper the ledger her father kept: every payment received, every entry annotated with a single word — 'amends.' The beat is grudging tenderness; both families were bound by the same secret arithmetic.

chapters.title: The Version I Was Told
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper confronts an aunt with the questions, and receives the official family story: a careless accident, settled privately, best forgotten. The beat is the suffocating weight of a lie maintained by everyone at once.

chapters.title: Inside the House Before It Sells
chapters.summary: Juniper and Hazel's alternating POV. The two break into the empty house and walk its rooms together, memories colliding — Juniper's bright version against Hazel's darker one. The beat is intimacy forged in contested territory.

chapters.title: The Room That Wasn't Repainted
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Behind a closet wall, Juniper finds scorch marks and a child's drawing signed by both girls — evidence the fire started inside the house, not the garage. The beat is the ground shifting under everything believed.

chapters.title: Who Struck the Match
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel admits what she has never said aloud: she saw nine-year-old Juniper near the flames that night and has carried the accusation silently ever since. The beat is betrayal resurfacing, threatening the fragile alliance.

chapters.title: The Middle of the Story
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Shattered, Juniper searches the mother's letters and finds a sealed envelope marked 'For J., when you stop being a tenant.' They cannot open it yet. The beat is suspended reckoning — the truth waiting on readiness.

chapters.title: Voss Makes an Offer
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Ms. Voss reveals the creditor's identity: the aunt, who needs the sale to cover debts of her own, and offers Juniper a quiet buyout to stop asking questions. The beat is temptation — justice priced like everything else.

chapters.title: Refusal in Writing
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper declines the buyout and instead files to delay the auction, forcing the estate's secrets into legal view. The beat is the first act of ownership — choosing the fight over the exit.

chapters.title: The Aunt Comes to Hazel Street
chapters.summary: Alternating POV. The aunt arrives to pressure Hazel into testifying that the debt was settled, and Hazel refuses, publicly, on her own porch. The beat is solidarity declared out loud, at cost.

chapters.title: For J., When You Stop Being a Tenant
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper opens the letter: the mother confesses she started the fire herself — a desperate act during the family's collapse — and let the Okafors believe anything rather than be seen. The payments were penance; the silence, shame. The beat is devastating release.

chapters.title: Telling Hazel First
chapters.summary: Juniper and Hazel's POV. Juniper reads the letter aloud to Hazel in the gutted garage. Grief, fury, and something like mourning-for-the-mother pass between them. The beat is truth offered without defense, and received without absolution — yet.

chapters.title: The Auction
chapters.summary: Multiple POVs. At the auction, Juniper stands among strangers bidding on their own childhood. The aunt's scheme collapses when the delay filing surfaces the unpaid amends. The house sells — to Hazel. The beat is public reckoning and private surrender.

chapters.title: What Cannot Be Cataloged
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. Juniper finishes the inventory at last, then burns the list in the Okafor backyard, keeping only three objects: the drawing, the ledger's last page, and the letter. The beat is letting go as an act of authorship over one's own story.

chapters.title: Amends, Continued
chapters.summary: Hazel's POV. Hazel asks Juniper to help restore the house — not as repayment, but as neighbors again. Juniper moves in temporarily, a tenant becoming a resident. The beat is cautious rebuilding, brick by chosen brick.

chapters.title: Owner of the Story
chapters.summary: Juniper's POV. One year later, on the restored porch, Juniper begins writing the true account of Hazel Street, reading the first page aloud to Hazel and the gathered odd family they've assembled. The beat is resolution: justice made outside the law, survival paid for honestly, home redefined as the people who stayed.
